title.narrative: Kvinna till kvinna GBV and women economic empowerment Serbia 2022-2026
Kvinna till kvinna GBV och kvinnors ekonomiska egenmakt Serbien 2022-2026

description.narrative: Kvinna till kvinna and partner organisations influence improvements in policy and practice regarding GBV and women's economic empowerment.
Kvinna till kvinna och samarbetsorganisationer påverkar förbättringar i policy och praxis när det gäller GBV och kvinnors ekonomiska egenmakt.

The objectives of the contribution are:
Overall Programme objective: Kvinna till Kvinna and partner organisations influence improvements in policy and practice regarding gender-based violence and womens economic empowerment in Serbia.
Specific objective 1 - Partner organisations and other relevant actors reached within the Project contribute to changes in attitude, practice and policy regarding GBV, based on the Istanbul Convention
Specific objective 2 - Organisations reached within the Project contribute to changes in policy and practice regarding womens economic empowerment.
Specific objective 3 - Increased sustainability and visibility of partner organisations and other relevant actors within the Project, and for their results

sector.narrative: Ending violence against women and girls
Women’s rights organisations and movements, and government institutions

description.narrative:
Some examples of results:
Intermediate Objective 1: Partner organisations and other relevant actors reached within the Programme contribute to changes in attitudes, practices, and policies regarding GBV, based on the Istanbul Convention.
Although the context in Serbia during 2025 was challenging due to the ongoing political crisis and stalled cooperation between civil society and state institutions, partner organisations nevertheless made significant contributions to advancing changes in attitudes, practices, and policies on gender-based violence (GBV) in line with the Istanbul Convention.
Through extensive service provisionincluding helplines, legal aid, and psychosocial supportthousands of women received essential assistance. At the same time, expanded outreach and diversified support channels improved accessibility for survivors. At the institutional level, accredited trainings on femicide prevention, along with ongoing cooperation with local actors, strengthened professional capacities and response mechanisms.
Advocacy efforts at both national and EU level highlighted key gaps in Serbias implementation of the Istanbul Convention and continued to push for legal reforms, particularly in relation to the Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence. In addition, systematic data collection and policy contributions supported more consistent and effective protection mechanisms for survivors.
Together, these efforts strengthened both direct support systems and broader accountability frameworks, while also raising awareness of GBV and institutional responsibilities.
Key Results from 2025
The Womens Counselling Centre (AWC) SOS hotline received 3,250 calls from 1,165 women (983 of whom were new clients). Due to flexible core funding, AWC was also able to provide 564 in-person counselling sessions with 130 women (87 new), as well as 310 email-based consultations offering emotional support, information, and referrals to other services for 182 women.
In total, 4,137 services were delivered, of which 2,403 (74%) related to psychosocial support and 847 (26%) to informational counselling. Legal aid services were provided to 793 survivors of violence (599 new), representing an increase of 109 beneficiaries compared to the previous reporting period. Altogether, 1,642 legal aid services were delivered, including 1,542 oral consultations (via telephone, email, in-person meetings at AWC premises, and messaging platforms such as Viber, WhatsApp, and Signal) and 100 written legal interventions.
In the area of institutional capacity building, AWC delivered accredited training on femicide prevention, approved by the Chamber of Social Protection. A total of 144 professionals from four citiesNovi Sad, Belgrade, Kragujevac, and Nicompleted the training.
Despite systemic challenges, the work of AWC during this reporting period once again confirmed its role as a key actor in implementing the Istanbul Convention, in a context where Serbian institutions continue to fall short of their obligations.
In synergy with the regional Sida-funded EU Advocacy Programme, AWC participated in the May 2025 advocacy week in Brussels. During this visit, AWC presented key findings and recommendations on GBV in Serbia, based on data from local womens civil society organisations. The presentation highlighted Serbias ongoing failure to implement the requirements of the Istanbul Convention, as well as challenges faced by AWC as a member of the working group on amendments to the Criminal Code and the Criminal Procedure Code concerning GBV offences. These issues were also situated within the broader context of the stalled Law on Gender Equality, currently pending before the Constitutional Court, and ongoing political instability in the country.
In 2025, the SOS telephone service operated by Womens Centre Uice continued to provide essential support, receiving a total of 888 calls. In addition, 122 individual psychosocial support consultations were delivered at the centres premises.
Legal information and assistance were provided to 29 women, including 120 telephone consultations, 45 individual consultations at the centre, and the preparation of 11 legal documents. Overall, 88 different women received support during the reporting period.
Throughout 2025, data collection and reporting activities continued in relation to the implementation of the Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence in the Zlatibor, Moravica, and Raka districts. Data was gathered from eight Basic Public Prosecutors Offices and five Police Administrations covering the period JanuaryDecember 2025. The purpose of this data collection was to enable comparison and analysis of the actions of state authorities, and to assess whether the law is being implemented in a consistent and coordinated manner. The ultimate objective is to ensure effective prevention of domestic violence and to guarantee urgent, timely, and efficient protection and support for victims.
During the reporting period, VDS supported and joined a joint response prepared by the Autonomous Womens Centre (AWC) on behalf of the Women Against Violence Network regarding proposed amendments to the Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence, specifically relating to two articles. The proposed changes aim to harmonise practices across a wider territorial scope under the jurisdiction of the Higher Public Prosecutors Office in Serbia.
Although the law stipulates equal rights and protection for all victims, implementation in practice remains uneven, resulting in significant disparities between different regions. In some areas, victims receive comprehensive support, while in others they receive minimal or no assistance. The proposed amendments are therefore intended to reduce secondary victimisation, improve procedural efficiency, strengthen proactive investigations, ensure trials within a reasonable timeframe, increase sentencing consistency, and establish a more uniform approach to proceedings. VDS submitted the AWC-prepared proposals to the Ministry of Justice during the public consultation process.
VDS also provided assistance and support to 119 victims, of whom 95 were women and 24 were men. The most common forms of victimisation were domestic violence (55.4%), violence in other contexts outside the family or workplace (15.9%), and workplace-related violence (11.7%).
Impuls from Tutin, the only autonomous womens and feminist organisation in that part of Serbia, continued its cooperation with institutions in Tutin and Novi Pazar engaged in combating gender-based violence. During the reporting period, 45 women contacted Impuls seeking support, of whom 37 required counselling and psychosocial assistance. Support included 275 telephone consultations, assistance in contacts with institutions in 12 cases, and referrals to legal aid organisations in 8 cases.
Intermediate objective 2 Organisations reached within the Programme contribute to changes in policy and practice regarding women's economic empowerment.
Overall, progress toward Intermediate Objective 2 demonstrates meaningful contributions by partner organisations in advancing policy and practice related to womens economic empowerment. Collectively, these initiatives contributed to both immediate improvements in womens economic participation and longer-term shifts in practices and awareness among key stakeholders.
In 2025 partner organisations have reached a total of 52 women through economic empowerment activities focusing on entrepreneurship (small scale business, income generating activities, mentorship, etc), and 109 on activities to increase employability (vocational training, skills development, etc). 43 women have been reached by activities aiming to decrease discrimination in informal and formal workplaces.
Key Results from 2025:
In 2025, Womens Centre Uice provided mentoring support to seven women from multiple vulnerable groups to help them exercise their social and labour rights. Women seeking assistance with employment were informed about and encouraged to use available measures provided by the National Employment Service (NES), including public works programmes, self-employment schemes, and work activation programmes. As a result of this support, five women were employed through the NES public works programme.
Requests related to the exercise of social rights primarily concerned work ability assessments and the acquisition of disability status, which are prerequisites for accessing permanent social assistance or disability pensions. Beneficiaries received individual support in navigating and completing the required administrative procedures.
In 2025, Retex continued its activities in the collection, donation, and recycling of second-hand textiles. Through its humanitarian service, a total of 121 socially vulnerable families received assistance in the form of clothing, footwear, and household textiles, including 30 Roma families and 15 individual beneficiaries. Funding was secured for four employed women at Retex, three of whom are women with disabilities. In addition, one further woman with a disability was engaged through the humanitarian service.
The Autonomous Womens Centre (AWC) participated in 71 employment mediation meetings for women with experience of violence. As a result, 32 women obtained employment, 27 completed prequalification programmes organised by the National Employment Service, and 12 women participated in economic empowerment training delivered by AWC.
ROZA from Zrenjanin received official accreditation from the Institute for the Improvement of Education and Training (ZUOV) for its curriculum aimed at educating secondary school staff on labour rights and human trafficking, with a particular focus on the gender dimension. This represents a significant step forward in strengthening young peoples knowledge of and access to economic rights.
ROZA developed the curriculum What You Need to Know Before Entering the Labour Market: Improving Teachers Competencies in the Field of Gender Equality, Human Trafficking, and the Labour Law Framework in cooperation with associates and external experts. The accreditation enables ROZA to equip teachers with the necessary tools and knowledge to inform students about their rights prior to entering the labour market.
During the reporting period, ROZA also developed two handbooks: one on labour rights for teaching staff and another on labour rights for students.
Intermediate objective 3 Increase sustainability and visibility of partner organisations and other relevant actors within the program, and their results.
Collectively, the efforts under Intermediate Objective 3 strengthened the sustainability of the womens movement, elevated the visibility of diverse actors, and fostered broader public engagement with gender equality issues.
Key Results from 2025:
AGC curated an intersectional and decentralised project for young women which included feminist trainings, mentorship from other feminist activists, and support in organising actions in their local communities. Educational training was organised in Vrnjaka Banja for sixteen young women activists and two peer educators. Through educational training, participants gained knowledge of the history of womens organisations, womens labour rights, the campaign for a living wage, how to organise a performance, and were provided with basic knowledge and tools for organising different types of activities (panels, workshops, street performances). After the training, they were motivated to form four informal groups and with the support of mentors. The long-term impact of this project is to get the young women participants involved in the womens movement, to contribute to its sustainability and longevity.
In the portfolio of partners, WFP project focused on visibility: for the womens movement, for diverse actors in the womens movement, and for WCSOs results. Throughout 2025 the organisation produced 12 TV reports, 12 online articles and texts, 5 TV shows and 5 video clips. All content produced for this project were on topics including, but not limited to GBV, gender equality, and WEE. With this, WFP contributed immensely to raising the visibility of the womens movement and various womens rights actors across the country. Many of the organisations that WFP highlighted in their various media and online outlets were local grassroots initiatives, rural groups, and other womens groups that are located outside of the capital city and very rarely have the opportunity to have their work presented in the media. These are also often smaller initiatives that fall outside of the greater womens movement that is often made up of bigger organisations and concentrated in urban centres and the capital city. Produced video clips were viewed 389,417 times on Facebook with a reach of 210,627. TV shows had 60,324 views on Facebook, , while the number of views on the YouTube channel is 743. Articles on web portal Foruminfo were read 3,367 times, 17,503 times on Facebook by 12,497 people, and engagement was 104. TV reports had 60,967views and engaged 133 people.
